General Electric's electronic-components factory in 1963 gave Shannon credibility. De Beers followed with an industrial diamond facility. Sony chose Shannon for its first European manufacturing operation.

General Electric established its Irish manufacturing subsidiary, the EI Company, in Shannon in 1963. Sony was manufacturing transistor radios there by 1963. De Beers' industrial-diamond business also established manufacturing operations in Shannon.

The aircraft leasing industry that emerged from Shannon represents perhaps the most unexpected success. Taking advantage of Ireland's tax treaties and regulatory environment, companies began using Shannon as a base for leasing aircraft to airlines worldwide. Today, Ireland is home to 14 of the world's 15 largest aircraft leasing companies, managing over 50% of the world's leased commercial aircraft fleet—a $500 billion industry that traces its origins to experiments in Shannon.

Aircraft leasing became another important Irish industry. Companies used Ireland's tax treaties and regulatory environment to lease aircraft to airlines worldwide. A December 2018 Irish government sector report stated that 14 of the world's 15 largest leasing companies had significant operations in Ireland, which held more than 60% of the global leasing market.

The Shenzhen Stock Exchange, established in 1990, started in a converted warehouse with hand-written transaction records. On opening day, crowds desperate to buy shares—any shares—rioted when allocation tickets ran out. The police had to use tear gas to disperse would-be investors. After decades of collective poverty, demand for ownership overwhelmed the orderly development of capital markets.

The Shenzhen Stock Exchange began trial operations on 1 December 1990. In August 1992, the sale of lottery forms for new-share subscriptions triggered unrest in Shenzhen. Demand for ownership put pressure on the institutions organizing the new market.

Consider the most basic infrastructure: electricity. Sub-Saharan Africa, with a population exceeding one billion, generates less electricity than Spain, with 47 million people. The entire installed capacity of 48 African countries is 68 gigawatts, compared to China's 2,000 gigawatts. Reliability compounds the shortage. Nigerian manufacturers report an average of 8 power outages per month. Ethiopian factories experience load shedding that can last entire days. Kenyan businesses spend 20% of their operating costs on backup power. No amount of tax incentives can compensate for having to generate your own electricity.

Electricity illustrates the infrastructure constraint. Using 2005 data, the World Bank reported 68 gigawatts of installed capacity across 48 sub-Saharan countries, including South Africa, comparable to Spain at that time. Reliability added a separate cost. Nigeria's 2014 Enterprise Survey reported 32.8 outages in a typical month. Firms interviewed in Kenya and Rwanda in late 2008 told the US International Trade Commission that generators increased electricity costs by 20–50%. Tax incentives leave companies to bear these operating costs.
